transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. [name]. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. [name]. Well, honestly, what really made me finally make an appointment is... I just keep getting up during these long sales strategy meetings at work. I know I'm supposed to stay seated, but I just can't seem to do it. I'll get up even if it's just to refill my water bottle or pace over by the printer for a minute. It's becoming an issue.

Can you tell me if you've experienced this kind of restlessness and trouble staying seated since you were a child, or is this something that's only started more recently, like in the past few months or years?

No, it's definitely not a new thing. Um, I remember this starting way before high school, actually. Back in elementary school, my teachers would always write notes on my report cards saying I was bright, but that I rushed through everything. They also pointed out that I talked out of turn a lot, forgot my homework... and I remember my desk was always just stuffed with half-finished papers. So, yeah, it's really been going on since I was a kid.
Aside from the restlessness, do you often find it hard to focus on tasks or conversations, or get easily distracted, even when you're trying to concentrate?

Yeah, I definitely do. Um, especially in those longer strategy meetings I mentioned, or when I'm reading through a client brief. I'll start out focused, but then after a few minutes... I just kind of realize I've been staring at the exact same slide or paragraph. I'll have absolutely no idea what the last point was, even though I'm really trying to pay attention to it.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversations or blurting out answers before someone finishes speaking?

Yeah, I do. Um, I actually do that quite a bit at work. I'll often jump in with an answer before a client or a coworker has even finished asking their question. And then... I'll realize I completely cut them off, or I end up answering the wrong thing because I didn't wait to hear the end of what they were actually asking.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates a longstanding (since elementary school) pattern of both inattentive symptoms (losing focus during meetings/reading, mind wandering, forgetting homework as a child, disorganized materials) and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms (inability to remain seated, pacing, interrupting others, blurting out answers). Symptoms are present across multiple settings (childhood school and current workplace) and cause functional impairment (disruption in professional meetings, miscommunication with clients/coworkers). The combined presence of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptom clusters, with childhood onset and cross-situational impairment, supports the combined presentation of ADHD (F90.2) rather than a predominantly inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive-only subtype.
